title: Ways to Pay
statement:
In a vending machine country there are **n** types of coins with values c[1], ..., c[n] (all different), and you have an unlimited supply of each type.

In how many different ways can you pay exactly **S**? Two ways are the same if they use the same number of coins of every type; the order of the coins does not matter. So 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are the **same** way.

The answer can be huge, so print it modulo 1 000 000 007 (10^9 + 7).
input:
The first line contains two integers **n** and **S**.

The second line contains n distinct integers c[1], ..., c[n].
output: Print one integer: the number of ways modulo 10^9 + 7.
hints: Let ways[v] be the number of ways to pay v. ways[0] = 1 (pay nothing).
To avoid counting 1+2 and 2+1 separately, put the loop over coin types outside and the loop over amounts inside.
editorial:
Dynamic programming over amounts: `ways[0] = 1`. Process the coin types one by one; for a coin c, go through v = c..S and do `ways[v] += ways[v - c]` (mod 10^9 + 7). After processing the first j coin types, `ways[v]` counts the combinations that use only those types, so every multiset of coins is counted exactly once. If the loops are swapped you count ordered sequences instead.

Complexity: O(n·S).
